addams: Jane Addams (1860–1935) was an American social reformer and philosopher in the pragmatist tradition, best known as the founder of Chicago's Hull House settlement and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate. Her philosophical work recasts democracy as a way of life grounded in sympathetic understanding, cooperation, and care across social divisions.
al-ghazali: Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111) was a Persian Islamic theologian, jurist, and Sufi mystic, widely considered one of the most influential thinkers in the Muslim tradition. His critique of Aristotelian philosophy, his reflections on doubt and certainty, and his meditations on evil and divine justice shaped centuries of debate about faith and reason.
audre-lorde: Audre Lorde (1934–1992) was an American poet, essayist, and Black feminist thinker who described herself as "black, lesbian, mother, warrior, poet." She argued that racial, sexual, and class differences should be acknowledged and used as sources of power rather than suppressed, and sharply criticized the silence and tokenism within mainstream feminism.
cavell: Stanley Cavell (1926–2018) was an American philosopher, long at Harvard, who extended ordinary language philosophy into readings of skepticism, literature, and film. He treated skeptical doubt not merely as an epistemological problem but as a condition of human relationships, and wrote influentially on Shakespeare, Hollywood comedy, and Emerson and Thoreau.
girard: René Girard (1923–2015) was a French-American philosopher and literary critic who taught at Stanford. He is best known for the theory of mimetic desire — the claim that we learn what to want by imitating others — and for the scapegoat mechanism, in which communities discharge their internal rivalries through collective violence.
h-richard-niebuhr: H. Richard Niebuhr (1894–1962) was an American Christian theologian and ethicist at Yale, brother of the better-known Reinhold Niebuhr. He is remembered for his typology of how Christ relates to culture, for the idea of "radical monotheism," and for an ethics of responsible, relational response to God and to other people.
irigaray: Luce Irigaray (born in Belgium in 1930 or 1932) is a French feminist philosopher trained in psychoanalysis, associated with the French feminist movement of the 1970s. In works like Speculum of the Other Woman she argues that Western philosophy has built its accounts of reason and subjectivity on an implicitly masculine model, leaving woman as the unthought other.
kendall-walton: Kendall Walton (b. 1939) is an American philosopher of art, long at the University of Michigan, known for the make-believe theory of representation. On his view artworks work as props in games of imagination, an approach he famously applied to the paradox of fiction — how we can genuinely feel for characters we know do not exist.
kropotkin: Pyotr Kropotkin (1842–1921) was a Russian geographer and naturalist turned revolutionary, and the leading theorist of anarcho-communism. Drawing on his observations of Siberian wildlife, he argued in Mutual Aid that cooperation, no less than competition, is a driving force of evolution and the foundation for a society without the state.
max-scheler: Max Scheler (1874–1928) was a German phenomenologist and the leading figure of the early phenomenology movement after Husserl. He developed a rich ethics of values and emotional life, studied love and sympathy, and — extending Nietzsche — gave the classic phenomenological analysis of ressentiment as the resentful self-deception of the powerless.
p-f-strawson: P.F. Strawson (1919–2006) was a British philosopher at Oxford, among the most important analytic philosophers of the twentieth century. His landmark essay "Freedom and Resentment" grounded moral responsibility in our everyday reactive attitudes — resentment, gratitude, forgiveness — while his book Individuals defended "descriptive metaphysics" against skeptical puzzles about persons and bodies.
warren: Karen J. Warren (b. 1947) is an American philosopher and one of the leading voices of ecofeminism. She argues that the domination of women and the domination of nature share the same oppressive logic — hierarchical, dualistic thinking about value — and that feminism and environmental ethics therefore need each other.
